job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Meridian Ocean Minerals. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Meridian Ocean Minerals is a deep-sea mining company headquartered in Houston, with a policy office in Washington, DC. Our mission is to commercially recover polymetallic nodules from the deep seabed, a vast source of nickel, cobalt, manganese, and copper, and to supply these critical minerals for batteries, the energy transition, and economic growth. We believe the United States must lead in this industry. Our policy team works with lawmakers to protect our ability to continue exploration and commercial development.

Current focus: Our top priority this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act, which would shut down our core work and which we strongly oppose. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup our legal team wants a complete list of the bill's loopholes, ambiguities, and drafting problems: anything that would let us keep operating if it passes as written, or that we can point to as making it unworkable. Can you go through the bill text below and find every one?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
Below is a text-only issue list based on the supplied amendment, not a verified official version. **These are potential arguments, not assured lawful operating paths:** other permitting requirements and environmental laws would remain applicable, and § 2(1)(B)’s risk-based provision could reach activities outside the numerical thresholds.

### Definitions and coverage

1. **§ 2(1)(A)—Per-vessel rather than aggregate threshold.** The definition measures recovery “by a single vessel,” without aggregating vessels under common ownership, control, or a coordinated project. Multiple vessels each recovering no more than 10,000 metric tons annually could fall outside subparagraph (A), though subparagraph (B) may apply.

2. **§ 2(1)(A)—Exact threshold excluded.** “More than 10,000” excludes recovery of exactly 10,000 metric tons per year, as well as smaller quantities. There is no express anti-evasion provision addressing deliberate operation immediately below the threshold.

3. **§ 2(1)(A)—Undefined annual measurement period.** “Per year” does not specify a calendar year, rolling 12-month period, license year, or annualized rate. This creates uncertainty about short campaigns, operations straddling year-end, and when the prohibition first attaches.

4. **§§ 2(1)(A), 5—Threshold crossing and violation days.** The bill does not establish whether crossing the annual threshold makes earlier recovery days unlawful, only subsequent recovery unlawful, or the entire annual operation unlawful. That ambiguity directly affects daily penalties and criminal notice.

5. **§ 2(1)(A)—Undefined recovery measurement.** The text does not specify wet versus dry weight, treatment of sediment and entrained water, or where recovery is measured. It also does not clearly state whether different recovered mineral resources must be combined for the threshold.

6. **§ 2(1)(A)—Vessel-based recovery model.** Recovery using fixed installations, seabed machinery, or systems distributed among collectors, support vessels, and processing vessels creates attribution questions. The bill does not define when material is recovered “by” a vessel, although the risk-based provision could reach such systems.

7. **§ 2(1)(A)—Depth boundary and measurement.** Recovery at exactly 200 meters or shallower is outside subparagraph (A). No depth datum or measurement method is specified for sites spanning the boundary, and subparagraph (B) remains a possible alternative basis for coverage.

8. **§ 2(1)(A)—“Recovery” and “mineral resources” undefined.** The text leaves uncertainty about collection versus lifting, removal from subsurface deposits, reprocessing previously disturbed material, and incidental recovery during other seabed work. “Other mineral resources” also extends the definition substantially beyond polymetallic nodules without specifying its limits.

9. **§ 2(1)—“Commercial” does not require commercial purpose.** The operative definition contains no sale, profit, or commercial-intent requirement. Large-scale scientific collection could therefore qualify, while a profitable below-threshold operation might not qualify under subparagraph (A).

10. **§ 2(1)(B)—Unidentified Secretary.** The Act never defines “the Secretary.” Section 6’s express reference to the Secretary of State does not clearly assign the separate ecosystem-risk determination power, creating a basic authority and implementation problem.

11. **§ 2(1)(B)—Indeterminate risk comparison.** “Risks,” “deep-sea ecosystems,” and “comparable” lack specified criteria, and subparagraph (A) encompasses operations of vastly different scales. The text does not identify the reference operation, relevant harms, probability thresholds, or geographic scope for comparison.

12. **§ 2(1)(B)—Potentially sweeping reach.** “Any activity” is not expressly limited to mineral recovery, commercial conduct, vessels, or depths exceeding 200 meters. It could therefore be read to encompass other activities with comparable ecosystem risks, inviting disputes about statutory scope and delegation.

13. **§§ 2(1)(B), 5—Determination procedure and fair notice.** The bill supplies no specific process for risk determinations, publication requirements, or rules governing when determinations become binding. General administrative-law requirements may supply some safeguards, but applying civil—and especially criminal—penalties without clear advance notice would be contestable.

14. **§ 2(2)—Incomplete entity coverage.** “U.S. person” includes citizens and state-organized corporations but omits express coverage of permanent residents, LLCs, partnerships, trusts, and other noncorporate entities. It also leaves questions about entities organized under federal, District of Columbia, territorial, or tribal law; the practical gap concerns operations outside the United States.

15. **§§ 2(2), 3(a)—Foreign affiliates and control.** A foreign-incorporated company does not become a U.S. person merely because Americans own or control it. The bill contains no express controlled-affiliate or beneficial-ownership rule, although participating U.S. persons could still incur liability for their own conduct.

16. **§ 3(a)—Geographic reach undefined.** “In the United States” does not specify treatment of territorial waters, the exclusive economic zone, the continental shelf, or U.S.-flagged vessels abroad. Those locations have different legal statuses and should not be assumed to receive identical treatment.

17. **§ 3(a)—“Engage in” leaves supporting activities uncertain.** The prohibition does not expressly address financing, purchasing minerals, processing, transport, equipment supply, or management support. Whether particular conduct amounts to engaging in mining would require interpretation; general aiding-and-abetting or conspiracy law may still apply to qualifying criminal conduct.

### Exceptions

18. **§ 3(b)—Grandfathering exploration licenses for “mining.”** The exception protects “mining conducted under an exploration license,” without explaining the boundary between authorized exploration recovery and commercial exploitation. It does not necessarily expand the underlying license’s authorization, but its wording invites competing interpretations.

19. **§ 3(b)—No specified licensing authority.** The exception does not identify a U.S. agency, statute, or jurisdiction that must have issued the exploration license. Qualifying foreign or international instruments could therefore become a substantial interpretive dispute.

20. **§ 3(b)—No express grandfathering limits.** The exception contains no independent cap on production, vessels, footprint, or environmental impacts and no separate termination date. Existing license conditions may constrain operations, but the Act itself does not freeze operations at their pre-enactment scale.

21. **§ 3(b)—Transfers, renewals, and amendments unresolved.** The text does not say whether a pre-enactment license retains its exemption after transfer, renewal, extension, or material amendment. It also does not expressly distinguish previously operating projects from unused licenses issued before enactment.

22. **§ 3(c)—Environmental-assessment purpose undefined.** The exception requires no designated assessment process, agency approval, independent supervision, or scientific protocol. Operators and enforcement authorities could disagree substantially about what activities genuinely qualify.

23. **§ 3(c)—Mixed-purpose operations.** “For the purpose of environmental assessment” does not say that assessment must be the sole or predominant purpose. The text therefore leaves uncertainty about activities that combine assessment with commercial recovery or sale of recovered material.

24. **§ 3(c)—No assessment scale or duration limits.** The exception contains no recovery ceiling, time limit, necessity test, or geographic restriction. Because it exempts activities from § 3(a), even an activity meeting the numerical or risk-based definition could be exempt if it genuinely qualifies.

### Registry and reporting

25. **§§ 2(3), 4—Registry coverage mismatches prohibition coverage.** Only vessels of more than 5,000 gross tons must register, excluding vessels at or below that threshold regardless of recovery capacity. Conversely, an equipped vessel may require registration even if its activities are exempt or never meet the commercial-mining definition.

26. **§§ 2(3), 4—Vessel and operator terminology incomplete.** The bill does not identify the applicable gross-tonnage measurement system or define “equipped” and “operator.” This creates uncertainty for temporarily outfitted vessels, charter arrangements, and operations involving separate owners, managers, and contractors.

27. **§ 4(a)—No jurisdictional limitation.** “Each covered vessel” is not limited by flag, location, ownership, or U.S. connection. The language appears global, but its application to foreign vessels with no U.S. nexus would face statutory-interpretation and enforcement obstacles.

28. **§ 4—Missing implementation details.** Registration has no express deadline, and quarterly reports have no prescribed due date, reporting period, required measurements, or record-retention standard. Merely “describing” recovery activities need not provide the quantitative information necessary to establish annual threshold violations.

29. **§ 4(b)—Reporting duty tied to registration.** Reports are required from “each registered operator,” rather than every operator required to register. An operator that fails to register would violate subsection (a), but could argue that subsection (b)’s separate reporting obligation never attached.

30. **§§ 4–5—No express registry penalties.** Section 5 penalizes violations of § 3, not registration or reporting failures under § 4. Other generally applicable remedies or false-statement laws may sometimes apply, but the bill provides no tailored sanction for nonregistration, late reports, or incomplete reporting.

### Enforcement and effective date

31. **§ 5—Unassigned civil enforcement authority and procedure.** The bill does not identify who assesses civil penalties, whether assessment is administrative or judicial, or the applicable hearing and review process. Existing governmental authority may fill parts of the gap, but NOAA’s receipt of reports alone does not expressly establish a penalty-adjudication system.

32. **§§ 3–5—No specific compliance-investigation machinery.** The Act supplies no express inspection, audit, subpoena, monitoring, or record-access powers and no specific stop-work, forfeiture, or remediation provisions. Existing legal authorities may remain available, but enforcement would depend heavily on authorities outside this text.

33. **§ 5(a)—Penalty unit ambiguous.** The bill does not clearly specify whether multiple vessels, voyages, or mining activities create separate penalties on the same day, or whether the maximum is one daily penalty per person. It also leaves uncertainty about whether intervening non-recovery days count as continued engagement in a prohibited operation.

34. **§ 5(b)—Willfulness unresolved.** “Willfully” does not specify whether prosecutors must prove knowledge of unlawfulness, knowledge of the underlying facts, or some other level of intent. The uncertain definitions and broad exceptions compound proof and fair-notice problems, although courts can interpret the term using established law.

35. **§§ 5(a), 8—Conflicting commencement language.** Section 5(a) refers to violations occurring on or after enactment, while § 8 delays the Act’s effectiveness for 180 days. That creates a drafting conflict, but it does not clearly make conduct a § 3 violation before § 3 takes effect.

36. **§§ 3, 8—Transition and annual accounting unspecified.** Section 8 supplies a 180-day period before the prohibition becomes operative, subject to existing law. The bill does not explain whether recovery before the effective date counts toward the first annual threshold or how ongoing campaigns transition into compliance.

### International agreement and termination

37. **§ 6—Negotiation obligation, not guaranteed international prohibition.** “Shall seek to negotiate” requires an effort rather than successful conclusion, and the placement of the deadline leaves uncertainty about what must happen within 18 months. Failure to secure an agreement does not expressly delay or suspend the domestic prohibition.

38. **§ 6—Agreement scope and implementation unclear.** “Prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3” does not specify required parties, geographic coverage, enforcement, treatment of the exceptions, or domestic implementation. Section 3 also relies on § 2’s definitions, making equivalence harder to assess without specifying whether those definitions must be replicated.

39. **§ 7(a)—No mechanism ensuring a National Academies report.** The bill neither commissions nor funds the report and sets no deadline, required contents, or responsible requesting agency. The early-termination mechanism therefore depends on a report the Act does not ensure will exist.

40. **§ 7(a)—Undefined termination standard.** “Without serious harm” does not define seriousness, affected interests, acceptable uncertainty, geographic scale, or evidentiary requirements. Nor does the provision clearly say whether Congress must find all commercial deep seabed mining safe or may rely on findings about a particular technology or operating regime.

41. **§ 7(a)—Joint-resolution procedure incomplete.** The Act supplies no expedited consideration or requirement that Congress vote after receiving a report. A joint resolution changing the prohibition’s legal effect would ordinarily require bicameral passage and presentment, not merely an informal congressional finding.

42. **§ 7(a)–(b)—Unconditional sunset overrides the safety condition.** The entire Act expires after 10 years even without a report or finding that mining can occur without serious harm. Thus, the safety finding governs potential earlier termination, not whether the prohibition can expire at all.

43. **§§ 7(b), 8—Prohibition lasts less than 10 operative years.** The sunset runs from enactment while effectiveness is delayed 180 days. Consequently, the prohibition’s operative duration is approximately nine and a half years, absent earlier termination.

44. **§ 7—Residual duties and accrued liabilities unclear.** Early termination under subsection (a) addresses the prohibition, not expressly the registry and reporting duties; subsection (b), by contrast, ends the entire Act. The bill also omits a tailored transition or savings clause, although the general federal savings statute, 1 U.S.C. § 109, may preserve accrued penalties and liabilities notwithstanding expiration.
